I thought it was worth going over some of the main points from this article.

It was a good read, and this is what I took from it ↓

1️⃣ Your income is part of your risk management

A regular income covers expenses and gives you fresh capital. You don't have to force trades, sell at a bad time, or depend on one position paying the bills.

The market doesn't work around your expenses.

2️⃣ Liquidity matters more than market cap

Market cap shows price × supply. It doesn't show how much you can sell near that price.

Check order-book depth, volume, circulating supply, upcoming unlocks, and where the token trades.

Public tokens offer more control than locked private deals, but only when enough liquidity exists to enter and exit properly.

3️⃣ Set your DCA rules before buying

Choose a max allocation and specific review points before building the position.

At each review, check product usage, revenue, token demand, competition, supply growth, and team execution.

DCA spreads out an entry, so it shouldn't turn into unlimited buying while the thesis gets weaker.

4️⃣ Large selloffs often have a mechanical side

Liquidations, thin order books, and forced selling can push a token far below the level suggested by the news.

That doesn't automatically make it cheap, however, it does mean that the price is reflecting market structure, not just fundamentals.

Look at liquidation data, open interest, order-book depth, onchain flows, and spot selling to see whether holders are leaving or leveraged traders are being forced out.

5️⃣ Use more than one exit trigger

Price is only one reason to reduce a position.

Portfolio weight, valuation, token unlocks, slowing adoption, and stronger competition can matter just as much.

Selling in stages makes it easier if you recover the initial capital, reduce exposure as the position grows, and keep a smaller amount for long-term.

6️⃣ More trading doesn’t always mean more progress

Jumping between narratives usually leads to extra fees, weaker entries, and decisions driven by FOMO.

Start journaling your trades. Write down why you entered, how you were feeling, what could prove the idea wrong, and what would make you sell.

Over time, you’ll start noticing patterns in your own behaviour. You’ll see which decisions came from a solid process and which ones came from fear, greed, or impatience.

Overall, surviving a bull market comes down to discipline. Protect your capital, understand what you own, and have a plan before emotions take over.

let's say you have eth or usdc, if you cash out to an exchange then you have to CGT anyway

instead let's say you transfer crypto to your card wallet and convert it to usdc, that's a CGT event for the same amount, and then you're getting a CGT event when you buy something and it converts the USDC -> AUD/whatever currency you pay in but then you're only paying CGT on the gain (or getting a loss) on the currency spread

so it's very minimal, based on what price you acquired USDC at and what the conversation rate between USD<->AUD is at the time of purchase, and i think it basically evens out over time

there's approx 1-1.5% in fx and other fees when you spend, but you'd be hit with fx fees when you convert to aud anyway

other cards ie etherfi offer 3% cashback up to like 50k a month of spend or something

plus you can have your stables earning yield while they're in a lot of these protocols

basically it's an awesome way to hold and spend some of your crypto assets imo - the convenience is epic, even if it was breakeven i would still do it, but i think it's a net positive too
